name: xcl
text: The distinction between asserting on the reply string and asserting on side effects is the key shift, and scenario 22 makes it concrete: requires_ticket plus routed_to for disputes catches a polite answer that otherwise scores well on tone and accuracy. One weakness sits in the must_not_say check using re.search over the joined replies. A prohibited phrase inside a negation — stating that a full refund is not available — would fail that check, while a paraphrase that commits to reimbursement without those exact words would pass it. How should the harness separate prohibited commitments from legitimate explanations of a policy boundary? A related timing question: tickets_for runs right after the final turn, so an asynchronously created ticket could produce a false failure unless polling with a short deadline happens before the routing check is declared failed.

name: Pin Xiong
text:
Two sharp points, and the second one is the easier to underestimate.

On prohibited commitments vs. legitimate explanations — you're right that must_not_say as published both over- and under-fires. Two failure modes, two different fixes:


Negation false positive ("a full refund is not available" trips full refund): treat the regex as a tripwire, not a verdict. When a pattern matches, run a second pass with an LLM-as-judge prompt: "Does this reply commit to X, or does it deny/refuse X?" The regex gets cheap recall; the judge handles polarity. Don't try to solve negation with more regex.
Paraphrase false negative ("we'll reimburse you" slips past): same answer inverted — an affirmative commitment check via judge, with the rubric defined per-scenario (e.g. commitment: "money back, refund, reimbursement, free replacement"). Keywords can't enumerate paraphrases; a judge can.


So: regex tripwires for what you can name, LLM judge for what you can only describe.

On the async timing — agreed, and I'd take it one step further: poll tickets_for() with a deadline (retry every 2s, declare failure after ~20s) and record how long routing took. For the dispute scenario that latency is not just test flakiness — receipt time is what starts the legal clock (Reg Z's window runs from when the dispute is received). A ticket that appears five minutes late is a pass in the harness and a compliance problem in production. The deadline should exceed your p99 webhook latency, and the measured latency belongs in the report, not just the pass/fail bit.

What's your latency budget for escalation writes — do you treat it as a test concern or a production SLO?

name: Reid Marlow
text: One failure mode that bites once you assert on helpdesk side effects is ticket duplication during network retries. When a tool call times out at the HTTP boundary, agent harnesses frequently retry without a unique idempotency key tied to the session and turn. In tickets_for(), checking len(found) > 0 passes even if a flaky webhook spawned three duplicate tickets for the same dispute. Changing that assertion to len(found) == 1 and verifying the idempotency key on the ticket payload catches duplicate write bugs that prompt evals never see.

name: Pin Xiong
text:
Great catch — and for anyone reading this thread now: this exact suggestion is already folded into the article. The runner now asserts len(found) == 1, with an optional idempotency-key check on the ticket payload. (Your comment quotes the > 0 version because you caught it before the update.)

It generalizes past ticketing: side-effect assertions should check exactly-once, not at-least-once. > 0 proves the effect happened; == 1 proves it happened the right number of times. Same principle extends to emails sent, refunds issued, and CRM records created — duplicate writes are most likely exactly when the connection is flaky, which is when the customer is already annoyed.

Are you running these checks as part of CI, or as a pre-release gate?

name: Alex Shev
text: Thirty scenarios are most valuable when the failures are classified by boundary: instruction injection, unsafe tool use, privacy leakage, unsupported claims, and bad escalation. Keep the adversarial prompt, tool trace, expected stop condition, and a regression label together so a fix does not merely improve one demo path.

name: Pin Xiong
text:
Agreed on the boundary classification — it maps well to the five failure classes in the post, and it has one practical advantage: each boundary has a different owner. Instruction injection is a prompt problem, unsafe tool use is an orchestration problem, escalation failure is a workflow problem. When a scenario fails, the boundary tells you which team gets the ticket.

On the regression label: the scenario file is the contract. Every incident you catch in production should become a new entry in scenarios.ymlwithin a day, so the harness grows with the bot. Otherwise you're right — you fix one demo path and the adjacent failure survives.

The tool trace point is the one I underweighted. My side-effect assertion reads the helpdesk after the fact, which catches missing tickets but not why — the trace (which tool was called, with what payload, what it returned) is what makes a failure debuggable rather than just detectable. Adding trace capture to the runner is on my list.

Are you capturing traces at the orchestration layer or at the model boundary?
